sentences.text: Tylocephale is a genus of dinosaur belonging to the group Pachycephalosauria, which is part of the larger clade Marginocephalia.
The only known species, T. gilmorei, was named by Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska in 1974.
This animal reached about 2 meters in length and weighed approximately 40 kilograms, making it average-sized for its group.
It is known from a skull that possesses the tallest dome among all pachycephalosaurids, along with parts of the lower jaw.
Unlike most dinosaurs which typically have three skull openings, Tylocephale bears only two, and its jugals feature giant, irregularly spaced tubers.
Behind the rounded cranial crest, the neck area displays an array of protruding spikes, nodes, and small bumps, while the preserved teeth show high crowns with arched cutting surfaces.
The specific name gilmorei honors American paleontologist Charles Gilmore for his first detailed description of a pachycephalosaur.
Fossils were unearthed between 1965 and 1971 by a Polish-Mongolian Expedition at the Khulsan locality within the Barun Goyot Formation of the Gobi Desert.
Maryańska and Osmólska formally described the genus and species as new in 1974.
Serrations on the dentition imply a potentially heterogeneous diet including leaves, nuts, seeds, and insects, though it is debated whether this mix is accurate.
It has been suggested that Tylocephale utilized a back-and-forth jaw motion, differing from the up-and-down motion seen in Stegoceras.
The skull dome is similar to Pachycephalosaurus, featuring fused sutures, mandibular and nasal tubercles, and expanded squamosal shelves.
It is debated whether older individuals of pachycephalosaurs like Tylocephale could engage in head-butting due to less vascularized domes and potential healing issues.
Recent phylogenetic analyses suggest Tylocephale is most closely related to Foraminacephale and Homalocephale.
Some researchers have suggested that Tylocephale gilmorei is a synonym of Prenocephale prenes.
A 2020 cladistic analysis suggested that pachycephalosaurs may extend back to the Early Jurassic.

The rock layers of the Barun Goyot Formation, where Tylocephale was found, date to the Early Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 71 million years ago, though the estimated time range for the genus itself is broader, from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
The time range for Tylocephale is estimated from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Tylocephale is endemic to the Barun Goyot Formation, which was deposited in alluvial plain, lacustrine, and aeolian environments under arid to semiarid climates.
